sents.text: Welcome back to Learn AI the Right Way.
In the last lesson, you learned what AI, machine learning and deep learning actually are.
Today we answer a very practical question: where will you actually do the work?
Every course in this series has hands-on labs.
You'll write code, run it, load data and save your results.
So before any of that, you need a place to work.
And here's the twist: the place you set up today is the same one you'll use for every course, and for real jobs too.
Think of a carpenter's workbench.
The tools hang in the same place every day.
Every job starts there, and nothing gets lost between jobs.
Your AI workbench is the same idea.
It has four parts: somewhere to write code, somewhere to run it, somewhere to keep your data, and somewhere that remembers your work.
Get those four right once, and you never set up from scratch again.
Your workbench can live in two kinds of place.
Online means in your web browser.
There's nothing to install, the computer is Google's, and you can often get a free graphics card for deep learning.
Offline means on your own laptop.
It works without the internet, it's private, and the tools are yours for good.
Neither is better.
We use both, and you'll set up each one in the next two lessons.
Here's the one rule that makes it all work.
All your code lives in one place: a repository called workbench, on GitHub.
A repository is simply a folder that remembers every change you make.
Because your work lives there, it opens unchanged in the browser, on your laptop, or inside a container.
Switch machines, switch jobs, lose a laptop: your work is safe.
